text: A kanger (Kashmiri pronunciation: [kãːɡɨr]; also known as kangri, kangid, or kangir)[1] is a traditional Kashmiri portable heater made of an earthen pot encased in wicker and filled with hot embers.[2] It is regarded not only as a practical source of warmth but also as a craft and art form.[3] Typically carried inside the pheran, a traditional Kashmiri cloak,[4] or wrapped in a blanket,[5] the kanger is primarily used during the cold winter period known as Chillai Kalan.[6] When used with modern clothing like jackets, it can serve as a hand warmer.[7] Standard kangers measure about 6 inches (15 cm) in diameter and can reach temperatures of approximately 150 °F (66 °C); they are available in various sizes, including smaller ones for children and larger ones for adults. After the earthen pots are molded and fired, artisans complete the wickerwork by adding two handles to hold the pot, propping the back with strong wicker sticks, and optionally coloring it to create an aesthetically delicate appearance.[8][9] It is commonly believed that Kashmiris learned the kanger from Italians who were part of the Mughal emperors’ retinue and visited the Valley during summer.[10] In Italy (where a similar device was called a scaldino)[11] and Spain, braziers were made in many shapes and were highly ornamented. However, historical evidence contradicts the claim that the kanger originated in Italy, though it was indeed used during the Mughal Empire era.[12] Visitors to Kashmir during winter are often surprised to see people carrying or placing fire pots in their hands or laps,[13] yet every Kashmiri is familiar with handling the kanger safely—its use is deeply rooted in tradition and remains in high demand, even in modern public and private offices. The kanger is widely used throughout Kashmir, especially in rural areas where power outages during winter are common,[14] and nearly every household owns at least one. In some urban homes, alternatives like hot water bottles, blowers, and electric blankets have replaced it. Aromatic seeds such as isband (Peganum harmala) are often burned in a kanger for ceremonial purposes.[15] Beyond Kashmir, people in the former Hill states of Himachal, Uttarakhand, and certain regions of Nepal also use local variants of the kanger. In 2015, a shopkeeper in Srinagar commissioned a kanger described as the world’s largest to attract customers to his textile shop; the size, exceeding one meter, presented significant technical challenges for wicker weavers.[16] Kangeris are crafted by small-scale farmers known as kanile. Charari Sharief is most renowned for a unique type called "charar kangir," while Anantnag is another major production center. The sector is unorganized but supported by various government schemes.[17][18] The Kashmiri proverb, "what Laila was on Majnun’s bosom (Legendary Lovers), so is the kanger to a Kashmiri," reflects the deep cultural bond between a Kashmiri and the kanger, as illustrated by the verse.[13] Frequent use of the kanger can lead to a specific skin cancer known as kangri cancer.[19] This condition was first documented by W. J. Elmslie in 1866 and was initially attributed to burns,[5] but current understanding suggests it results from a carcinogenic distillation product of woodcoal.[20][contradictory] The tourism department of Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) has officially decided to celebrate 'Pheran and Kangri Day' on February 19 to promote Kashmiri culture.[21]
